documents: Möller, Friedl, Palmer & Marzeion (2022), JGR Earth Surface 127, e2021JF006302, published PDF (25 pp.)

entry.evidence: However, until now a lack of knowledge regarding processes at the grounding lines of the two basins has hampered this full understanding.

steps.action: The authors take from earlier aerial and satellite velocity studies that basins 2 and 3 accelerated and then slowed, which suggested a surge.
steps.quote: basins 2 and 3 of FIIC were also suggested to be of surge type

steps.action: The authors take from earlier observations (undulating surface, flat-topped icebergs, salinity, low elevations) that the basins form a floating ice shelf.
steps.quote: basins 2 and 3 were finally suggested to form floating tongues

steps.action: They pose the aim: analyse grounding line migration and ice discharge variability of basins 2 and 3, then discuss surge triggers and ice-shelf stability.
steps.quote: [...] this study is to contribute to closing this gap by conducting an in-depth analysis of the marine-terminating parts

steps.action: They produce 2015–2020 annual Sentinel-1 velocity mosaics by intensity tracking of more than 700 SAR acquisitions, with a correlation threshold, a three-step filter and SNR-weighted averaging.
steps.quote: We produced six annual ice surface velocity mosaics of FIIC for the years 2015–2020 by averaging dense time series

steps.action: They correct the velocity fields for residual co-registration error by calibrating against median velocities over stable ice-free ground.
steps.quote: by calibrating our range and azimuth velocities against median velocities measured over ice-free ground

steps.action: They delineate the basin boundaries by manual digitization from Sentinel-1 2019 flow directions and ArcticDEM elevations.
steps.quote: We delineated the boundaries of basins 2 and 3 in the interior of FIIC by manual digitization

steps.action: They map grounding line proxies for eight dates: the tidal-flexure hinge line from Sentinel-1 DInSAR (2018, 2021) and surface-slope breaks from five Landsat scenes (1993–2019).
steps.quote: we localized the approximate grounding lines by applying one dynamic and two static remote sensing methods for grounding line proxy mapping

steps.action: They apply hydrostatic equilibrium to the OIB surface elevations with standard ice density to identify floating sections, and find large sections that appear grounded.
steps.quote: we aimed to identify floating shelf ice sections, but found large sections of grounded ice

steps.action: Trusting prior evidence that the shelf floats, they revise the density auxiliary, compute the critical density needed for flotation along the tracks, and adopt 875 kg m−3.
steps.quote: we considered that the ice shelf density is likely to be lower than the maximum value used above

steps.action: They compute ice discharge through idealized flux gates from BM3/ArcticDEM thickness and gate-normal velocity (0.9 × surface velocity), separately for each velocity dataset.
steps.quote: We calculated ice discharge (D) through these idealized flux gates by integrating the product of ice thickness (h)

steps.action: They check the reduced density against the literature range for crevassed ice, against FIIC ice-core densities, and against firn cover in the spring DEM.
steps.quote: It also fits well with density data from an ice core drilled near the summit of FIIC in 2006

steps.action: They compare BM3 with independent OIB bed elevations and with the DInSAR evidence of floating ice, conclude that the BM3 uncertainty is overestimated and the sub-shelf bed is too high, and construct a reduced bed uncertainty.
steps.quote: Root mean square differences between BM3 and OIB bed elevations below the ice shelf amount to just ±8.9 m a.s.l. (basin 2)

steps.action: They propagate the bed, velocity-dataset and velocity-conversion uncertainties into the discharge uncertainty.
steps.quote: we calculated ice discharge uncertainty across each flux gate cross section

steps.action: They quantify the grounding line positions over time along the OIB tracks: a slight advance in 1993–1999, then retreat of 2.2 ± 1.3 km (basin 2) and 2.7 ± 0.9 km (basin 3) by 2019, at differing rates.
steps.quote: We analyzed the variability of the grounding line locations over time and identified retreat in both basins

steps.action: They check the Landsat-based retreat rates and grounding zones against Sentinel-1 rates for 2018–2021 and against the OIB buoyancy-derived grounding line of 2015.
steps.quote: which suggest similar retreat rates of 0.295 ± 0.258 km a−1 in basin 2

steps.action: They estimate mean annual discharge for the pre-surge, surge and post-surge periods and the 1988–2020 totals, finding post-surge reductions of 90% and 96%.
steps.quote: This means, that ice discharge decreased by 90% after the surge in basin 2 and by 96% in basin 3.

steps.action: They describe the changing flow regime: shifts in velocity-maximum elevations and the appearance and deactivation of flow branches across the surge phases.
steps.quote: The observed variability in ice flow regimes between pre-surge, surge and post-surge periods involved distinct changes

steps.action: They state the rival surge mechanisms from the literature: the thermal switch (Svalbard-type) and the hydrological switch.
steps.quote: there are two different theories of glacier surges (Sevestre, 2015)

steps.action: They compare the observations with Svalbard-type traits: the cold base, draw-down and modest speed-up agree, while the rapid slowdown, the grounding line advance and the lack of meltwater disagree.
steps.quote: At first glance, the evidence we present for FIIC points to the former theory

steps.action: They reject ocean forcing as the trigger: ERA5 sea surface temperature and sea ice were stable, and the expected grounding line retreat did not occur. Subsurface warming is left open.
steps.quote: Ocean conditions in terms of sea ice concentration and sea surface temperatures in front of NW FIIC were stable over the study period

steps.action: Given the conflicting evidence, they refine the explanation to Svalbard-type surges modified by ice-shelf buttressing, which thickened the ice and advanced the grounding line.
steps.quote: To overcome this context of conflicting evidence we here propose a modifying role of the ice shelf

steps.action: They set aside subglacial lake drainage as the water source for lack of any indication.
steps.quote: there are no indications that such a process might have played a role in the surges

steps.action: They frame grounding line retreat over retrograde beds as buoyancy-driven instability opposed by ice-shelf buttressing that differs between the basins.
steps.quote: The resulting increase in the buoyancy forces suggests a positive-feedback response in both basins implying dynamic instability

steps.action: They relate the post-2014 divergence in retreat rates to the sea ice loss (ERA5, Landsat) and to the lateral confinement that exists only in front of basin 3.
steps.quote: the impact of sea ice reduction on the grounding line is suggested to be more severe in front of basin 2

steps.action: From grounding line theory they derive expectations for future grounding line stability and ice-shelf persistence.
steps.quote: With further retreat the grounding lines will approach the prograde-sloping, rear parts of the submarine troughs

steps.action: They compare the derived shelf thickness (69.7 ± 25.5 m) with the independent salinity-based estimate (~45 m) and with the earlier flotation evidence.
steps.quote: which agrees within uncertainty with the thickness of ∼45 m which has been suggested by Bendtsen et al. (2017)

steps.action: They compare the discharge and surge velocities with Devon, Agassiz and Austfonna ice caps and with the near-zero mass balance of FIIC.
steps.quote: the ice discharge from basins 2 and 3 of FIIC during the period 1988–2020 was small when considering the Arctic-wide perspective

steps.action: They retain the first grounding line maps, the retreat values and the discharge estimates with uncertainties, together with the modified Svalbard-type interpretation.
steps.quote: We carried out the first grounding line mapping at the outlet basins 2 and 3 of Flade Isblink ice cap

tree.answer: Surges and grounding line migration of two ice-shelf-terminating basins; suggested by prior data
No; grounding lines are known from proxies and discharge is inferred
Map grounding lines and quantify discharge; explain surges
Thermal vs hydrological switch; ocean forcing; subglacial lake drainage
Partly: Svalbard-type predicts gradual slowdown and lower thinning; ocean forcing predicts retreat
Found: one surge cycle recorded in archived satellite data
Partly: independent Sentinel-1, OIB and literature checks; large discharge uncertainties
Estimates kept; modified Svalbard-type as best explanation; trigger unresolved

end.claim: The grounding lines of basins 2 and 3 advanced slightly in 1993–1999 and then retreated 2.2 ± 1.3 km and 2.7 ± 0.9 km by 2019; ice discharge totalled 1.85 ± 1.59 Gt and 1.38 ± 1.22 Gt over 1988–2020 and fell by at least 90% after the 1996–2001 surges.

decisive_move.sentence: Without mapping grounding line proxies for several dates from Landsat surface slope and Sentinel-1 DInSAR tidal flexure, there would be no retreat record, no flux gates and no discharge estimate.

gates.evidence: All data were archived remote-sensing products chosen by availability and cloud-free contrast, not directed by a hypothesis (p. 4). The Svalbard-type hypothesis met contrary evidence (p. 19) and was modified rather than rejected. The estimates were checked against Sentinel-1, OIB and the salinity-based thickness (pp. 15–16, 21). The density, factor and thresholds were set empirically or after seeing the data (pp. 5, 10); nothing was pre-registered.

imports.item: Standard error propagation and quadrature combination of independent uncertainties
Theory of buttressing suppressing marine ice sheet instability (Pegler 2018, J. Fluid Mech.)

novelty_claims.quote: We determined, for the first time, the grounding line locations of these basins and analyzed their variability with time.
We carried out the first grounding line mapping at the outlet basins 2 and 3 of Flade Isblink ice cap
we carried out the first quantification of ice discharge and its variability from the two basins

limits: Sub-claims sit at different statuses. The characterization of the surges as Svalbard-type modified by buttressing is best_explanation: it was adopted after conflicting evidence, and the water source for surge initiation is admitted as unresolved. The differing buttressing (sea ice loss, lateral confinement) as the cause of the divergent post-2014 retreat rates is best_explanation by argument, with no model test. The statements on future stability are qualitative expectations, not forecast_skill. Discharge uncertainties are nearly as large as the values (1.85 ± 1.59 Gt). Discharge for 1993–1995 and 2002–2004 is interpolated. Topography, flux gates and flow direction are held time-invariant, and seasonal variability is ignored. Subsurface ocean warming was not investigated. Process not shown by the document: how the five Landsat scenes and the 0.08 correlation threshold were chosen beyond 'empirically'; whether the manual digitization of grounding lines and boundaries was repeated or checked by a second analyst (inference: apparently not); and the order in which the density value was fixed relative to the discharge results. The 875 kg m−3 density was chosen post hoc to make basin 3 float. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown. The composition is coded trace_series for the surge explanation, but the headline claim is an estimate, so the fit is partial.

disagreements.target: Cook (2016), surplus surface meltwater as the water source for cryo-hydrologic warming
disagreements.support: Modeled surface mass balance (Rinne et al., 2011) shows below-average melt during the surge period.
disagreements.quote: However, modeled surface mass balances of FIIC reveal below average summer melt over the surge period (Rinne et al., 2011), which makes this source unlikely.

disagreements.target: Typical Svalbard-type surge cycle (Melvold & Hagen 1998; Murray et al. 2003)
disagreements.support: The rapid post-surge slowdown and the grounding line advance at FIIC depart from the gradual deceleration and lower-glacier thinning of the standard model, so a buttressing modification is proposed.
disagreements.quote: At basins 2 and 3, the transition between surge and post-surge velocities appeared to be much faster (Figure 8).

disagreements.target: BedMachine v3 bed elevation uncertainty grid (Morlighem et al., 2017)
disagreements.support: Small RMS differences between BM3 and independent OIB bed elevations along the flight tracks.
disagreements.quote: suggests that the BM3 bed elevation uncertainty grid considerably overestimates the actual uncertainties across the grounding zones of both basins

disagreements.target: BedMachine v3 sub-shelf bed elevations (Morlighem et al., 2017)
disagreements.support: Sentinel-1 DInSAR interferograms show floating ice where BM3 implies grounded ice.
disagreements.quote: This suggests a significant but unquantifiable overestimation of bed elevations by BM3 data in this area

disagreements.target: Standard glacier ice density of 917 kg m−3 used in ice discharge studies (e.g., Mankoff et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: OIB buoyancy calculations require a lower density for flotation, and the lower value is consistent with ice-core densities and firn cover.
disagreements.quote: This value is lower as the standard glacier ice density (917 kg m−3) usually assumed in ice discharge calculations

disagreements.target: ITS_LIVE automatically generated velocity mosaics, 1992–2014 (Gardner et al., 2018, 2019)
disagreements.support: Patchy grids, physically unrealistic magnitudes and large voids over FIIC.
disagreements.quote: the automatically generated ITS_LIVE mosaics were deemed error-prone across large parts of FIIC

disagreements.target: Ice thickness corrections in previous discharge calculations (Mankoff et al., 2020; Sánchez-Gámez et al., 2019)
disagreements.support: Elevation change rates for FIIC exist only since 2000, and alternating thinning and thickening prohibit extrapolation.
disagreements.quote: In our case, we regard this as more appropriate than an inclusion of ice thickness corrections

alternatives_considered.chosen: MEaSUREs and DInSAR velocities for 1992–2014; ITS_LIVE for 1988–1992 and 2014–2018
alternatives_considered.reason: The 1992–2014 ITS_LIVE mosaics are error-prone over FIIC; the 1988–1992 errors lie outside the study area, and no alternative data exist

alternatives_considered.chosen: Three grounding line proxy methods (tidal DInSAR, surface slope, hydrostatic), treated separately
alternatives_considered.reason: DInSAR is more accurate; Landsat gives longer coverage; OIB covers the flight tracks

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Standard 917 kg m−3; minimum critical 830 kg m−3
alternatives_considered.reason: The minimum density that floats the basin 3 shelf; consistent with ice-core densities and firn cover

alternatives_considered.chosen: Conservative intermediate bed uncertainty constructed from BM3 and OIB
alternatives_considered.alternatives: BM3 uncertainty grid; OIB ±10 m uncertainty
alternatives_considered.reason: The BM3 grid overestimates the uncertainty where OIB constrains the bed

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Ice thickness corrections from elevation change rates; time-varying flux gates
alternatives_considered.reason: Elevation change exists only since 2000 and alternating regimes prohibit extrapolation; a single gate per basin follows earlier studies
Direction changes occur mainly in slow-flow areas with negligible discharge

alternatives_considered.chosen: Svalbard-type surge modified by ice-shelf buttressing
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Hydrological switch; ocean forcing; subglacial lake drainage; subsurface ocean warming
alternatives_considered.reason: Cold-based ice, draw-down and modest speed-up; stable ocean conditions; no lake-drainage indication
